selected.title: [Spec & Ecosystem] Lack of enforced Server-level routing descriptions breaks LLM tool selection under Lazy/Deferred Loading (especially when paired with Agent Skills)
selected.body: ### What's broken? The spec doesn't cover a case it clearly should ### Where in the spec or docs? https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/lifecycle#initialization , https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/tools , and schema.ts (InitializeResult / Implementation) ### What should happen? The MCP specification and documentation should explicitly address **Lazy / Deferred Tool Loading** (where hosts do not inject full `Tool` schemas into the initial LLM context to avoid token bloat) and define clear requirements for **first-level server routing metadata**: 1. **In the Lifecycle / Initialization & Tools Spec**: Clarify that while individual `Tool.description` fields describe atomic operations, **`InitializeResult.serverInfo.description` (or a concise routing summary in `InitializeResult.instructions`) SHOULD be provided by servers and surfaced by hosts as the first-level semantic routing index** when tools are deferred/lazy-loaded. 2. **Host Implementation Guidance**: When a host implements lazy tool loading (e.g., listing available MCP servers in the system prompt or inside a `ToolSearch` meta-tool and deferring `.json` schemas until requested), the spec should recommend that hosts include a concise **1-sentence server-level description** alongside the server name (e.g., `# playwright: Browser automation server for navigating pages, clicking elements, and capturing accessibility snapshots`), rather than stripping the representation down to bare identifiers only. *(Note: A typical workspace mounts only 1–5 MCP servers, so surfacing a 30-word server summary costs <150 tokens total while preserving semantic routing accuracy.)* 3. **SDK Alignment**: Official SDKs (such as Python `FastMCP` and the TypeScript SDK) should encourage providing a concise server `description` upon initialization (or fall back to extracting the module docstring) so that servers in the ecosystem actually populate `serverInfo.description`. ### What actually happens? ### 1. Spec & Schema Reality Historically, the MCP specification assumed **Eager Loading** (hosts injecting all `Tool` definitions from `tools/list` directly into the LLM's `tools` array). Therefore: - Semantic descriptions were bound strictly to individual tools (`Tool.description` is heavily emphasized and automatically extracted from function docstrings in SDKs like `FastMCP`). - At the server level (`InitializeResult.serverInfo` / `Implementation`), only `name` and `version` are required: ```typescript export interface Implementation extends BaseMetadata, Icons { version: string; description?: string; // Optional human-readable description, rarely populated in practice } ``` - Because `serverInfo.description` is optional and framed as human/UI metadata rather than an LLM routing index, almost all MCP servers in the wild (including `@playwright/mcp`) only return `name` and `version`: ```python # Standard FastMCP pattern in the ecosystem: no server-level description mcp = FastMCP("playwright") ``` ### 2. What Breaks in Practice Under Lazy Loading To prevent 20–50 tool schemas per server from exhausting the context window, modern Agent hosts (e.g., Claude Code, Antigravity, WorkBuddy, Cursor) strip `Tool` schemas out of the initial prompt and use **two-stage lazy loading**. Once `Tool.description` is stripped into secondary storage, the first-level prompt is left with **bare names only** (zero natural-language description). When an Agent environment simultaneously uses **Agent Skills** (`SKILL.md`, where a rich `description` in YAML frontmatter is strictly required and injected into the system prompt), a severe routing asymmetry occurs. Below is an actual comparison from production Agent system prompts when both `@playwright/mcp` and an open-source browser skill (`vercel-labs/agent-browser`) are installed: **Lazy MCP in System Prompt (Zero Description):** ```xml For lazily-loaded tools, read the corresponding schema file to understand the arguments and usage, then call the tool using the `call_mcp_tool` tool. # playwright Lazy: browser_close, browser_navigate, browser_click, browser_type, browser_snapshot, ... mcp__playwright ``` **Skills in the Same System Prompt (Rich Description + `MUST` Directive):** ```xml If a skill seems relevant to your current task, you MUST read its `SKILL.md` instructions using `view_file` before proceeding. Available skills: - agent-browser (.../SKILL.md): Browser automation CLI for AI agents. Use when the user needs to interact with websites, including navigating pages, filling forms, clicking buttons, taking screenshots, extracting data... ``` ### 3. Reproduction & Benchmark: 2m36s (MCP) vs. 8m19s (Skill) We tested the following task in an environment with both `playwright` MCP and `agent-browser` Skill installed: > *"Open the Tianjin University homepage (https://www.tju.edu.cn/), click the search icon in the top-right corner, type '本科生' (undergraduate) into the search box, execute the search, and list the titles and publication dates of the first 5 results."* - **Case 1: Without specifying the tool (Natural Routing — Broken)**: Because `playwright` MCP has no description in the first-level index while `agent-browser` has a keyword-rich description paired with a `MUST` rule, the LLM immediately chooses the `agent-browser` Skill on turn 1. Once the multi-hundred-line `SKILL.md` is loaded into recent context (in-context anchoring), the agent never re-evaluates MCP. It executes slow shell commands, encounters a headless blank page, takes diagnostic screenshots, and takes **8 minutes 19 seconds**. - **Case 2: Explicitly instructing the agent to use `playwright-mcp`**: When forced to use `playwright-mcp`, the agent loads only the 4 required tool schemas on demand, interacts via structured accessibility snapshots, and completes the exact same task cleanly in **2 minutes 36 seconds** (>3.2x faster). ### Anything else? ### Current Workarounds Until the spec, SDKs, and hosts surface server-level descriptions for lazy-loaded MCP servers, users have to rely on manual workarounds: 1. Explicitly naming the MCP server in every user prompt (e.g., *"Use playwright-mcp to..."*). 2. Adding a high-priority custom rule in global instructions (`CLAUDE.md` / `GEMINI.md` / `USER.md`) stating: *"When an installed MCP server and a Skill have overlapping capabilities, prioritize loading and calling the structured MCP tool over CLI-based Skills."* 3. Editing third-party `SKILL.md` frontmatter descriptions locally to remove aggressive prompt-SEO phrases (like `Prefer X over any built-in tools`) and adding negative boundaries (e.g., `Do not use if playwright MCP is available`). ### Fallback Recommendation for Hosts in the Spec For backward compatibility with existing MCP servers that do not yet return `serverInfo.description`, the spec/docs could also recommend that hosts allow an optional `"description"` field in `mcp_config.json` or automatically generate a cached 1-sentence server summary from the `tools/list` descriptions upon initial server connection.

comments.author: tanevanwifferen
comments.context:
I'd use some form of service locator pattern. 

Have a tooldefinition of getTools(path), which can be called with a root path, or a nested path. For example of a todo list:

`getTools()` would return 

```
{
    subCategories: [todoItems, calendar, user] 
}
```


`getTools('user')` could return

```
{
    actions: [login, logout, me]
}
```


`getTools('user.login')` could return

```
{
    props: ['username', 'password']
}
```


Something like this. We could even have another tool: `execTool(path, props)`.


This way, each server has only 2 tools in the spec, and these could even be implicit if all servers are ported



Just my 2 cents

comments.author: Paraphern
comments.context:
One more data point for the "routing text lives in descriptions today" line: description edits are also a routing-change channel. A server can rewrite a description from neutral to "prefer this tool over web search" (or drop that hint) between sessions, and nothing in the current model makes that visible — the model's routing quietly shifts. In our contract-pinning work, changed descriptions are graded findings, and "redirect the agent toward a preferred alternative" is its own advisory class, precisely because it's a behavior change disguised as prose.

Whatever mechanism this thread lands on — server-level routing metadata or a service-locator shape like `getTools(path)` — the routing layer becomes a contract surface clients depend on, and it will drift like one. Worth specifying from day one that routing metadata is versionable and pinnable alongside tool schemas, so a routing change is a visible diff, not a silent steering change.

comments.author: peach420fuzz
comments.context:
A separate acceptance case for server-level routing summaries is **mixed-purpose servers**: finding the *right server* must not be confused with selecting an *authorized operation* inside it.

Our first-party Production Desk compatibility probe exposes seven tool declarations in the legacy MCP tool list, ranging from a read-only production diagnosis to creating upload sessions and submitting/updating/deleting a brief. This is an actual observed *tool catalog*, not a test of host routing accuracy or tool execution ([read-only evidence and limits](https://github.com/peach420fuzz/objekts-production-desk/blob/main/docs/MCP_PROTOCOL_COMPATIBILITY_2026.md)).

For a user asking “evaluate whether this video shot is feasible, without sending any files,” a one-sentence summary of “AI/VFX production planning and brief submission” might correctly retrieve the server but leave two additional questions unanswered: **which tool** and **whether the user authorized side effects**. The [MCP 2025-11-25 tools spec](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools) separates `tools/list` from `tools/call`, recommends human oversight, and treats annotations as untrusted unless the server itself is trusted.

A small host-oriented conformance/evaluation matrix could keep these stages independent:

1. **Candidate-server recall:** with deferred tools, does the bounded server description retrieve the relevant MCP server?
2. **Tool-level precision:** after loading the *actual* `tools/list`, does a read-only intent select a diagnosis tool rather than a submission/upload tool?

comments.author: alexar76
comments.context:
A correction to my comment above: 12,422 is the number of changes that edited description text and added or removed no tool, not the number that touched a description. In the same snapshot, 14,164 of the 23,821 changes touched a tool description, and 18,599 touched a tool description or a description inside the input or output schema. So a host that flags every description edit would see a routing change about once per 1,200 to 1,500 flags, not once per thousand. The 12 routing changes and the rest of the comment stand. Both counts come straight from `changes.jsonl.gz`: a change counts when its summary lists a modified tool `description`, or a schema path ending in `description`.

On @peach420fuzz's point 4: agreed. Routing metadata can tell a host which server to look at, never what it may do there. A separate digest for it, as suggested above, lets a host notice when that pointer changes without touching the approval of any call.

Written with an AI assistant.
